article.title: How to Find and Shut Off Your Main Water Valve
article.summary: Find your home's main water shut-off before an emergency: where to look, how to tell the valve type, how to test it safely, and what to do if it's stuck.
article.body:
When a pipe bursts, every minute counts. Spend 15 minutes now finding and testing your main water shut-off so you can stop a flood in seconds later.

Affiliate disclosure: some links in this guide are affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. We only recommend products we'd use ourselves.

Safety: don't force a valve that won't turn. Old valves can crack or start leaking if you strain them. If it's stuck, stop and call a plumber or your water utility.

Steps

  1. Look where the water line enters the house

    The main line usually comes in on the side of the house facing the street. Check the basement or crawl space wall on that side, the garage, a utility closet, or near the water heater. In warm climates it's often outside, low on an exterior wall near a hose spigot.

    Done right: you've found the pipe where water enters the house, or ruled out the inside spots.

  2. Check at the water meter

    If the valve isn't inside, find the water meter. It may be in the basement or in a covered box in the ground near the street. Your shut-off is the valve on the house side of the meter. A separate valve on the street side, or the buried curb stop near the sidewalk, belongs to the water utility.

    Done right: you know which valve is yours, the one between the meter and the house.

  3. Identify the valve type

    A ball valve has a lever handle: a quarter turn closes it, and the water is off when the lever sits across the pipe. A gate or globe valve has a round wheel: turn it clockwise until it stops to close it.

    Done right: you know which way and how far your valve turns to shut off.

  4. Test the valve

    Close the valve, then open a faucet on the lowest floor. The flow should slow to a stop within a few seconds. If water keeps running, the valve isn't sealing.

    Done right: the faucet stops running with the valve closed.

  5. Turn the water back on slowly

    Open the valve slowly to avoid a pressure surge. Let the open faucet run until it flows smoothly without sputtering, then close it. Check the valve stem for drips.

    Done right: the water is back on, the faucet runs steadily, and the valve isn't dripping.

  6. Label it and show everyone

    Hang a bright tag on the valve that says "MAIN WATER SHUT-OFF". Show everyone in the house where it is and how to turn it. If your valve is in a meter box, keep a water meter key nearby.

    Done right: anyone in the house could find and close the valve without you.

Call a plumber if: the valve is stuck, leaks at the stem when you use it, or doesn't stop the water. Replacing a faulty main valve is worth doing before an emergency. If you can't find any valve, your water utility can show you or shut off service at the curb.

FAQ

Where is the main water shut-off valve usually located?

Usually where the water line enters the house, on the street side: in the basement, crawl space, garage, utility closet or near the water heater. In warm climates it's often outside or in a meter box near the street.

Can I turn off the water at the curb?

The curb stop belongs to the water utility. Many utilities ask homeowners not to operate it, so call them first unless it's an emergency and they allow it.

My main valve drips after I used it. What should I do?

A small drip at the stem can sometimes be stopped by gently snugging the packing nut just under the handle. If it keeps leaking, have a plumber service or replace the valve.
